title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data

paper.title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
paper.abstract: Abstract Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation–action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 𝟔𝟏 % \mathbf{61\%} reduction in compatibility error—which measures consistency under transformation composition—relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48 % 80.48\% to 85.12 % 85.12\% , with per-task gains up to 9.66 \mathbf{9.66} percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Symmetry can improve sample efficiency and generalization in robot policy learning by allowing experience to be shared across equivalent task configurations [ 22 , 12 , 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 , 6 , 9 ] . Exploiting this structure requires coupled observation–action transformations, which existing symmetry-aware methods typically assume are known. This assumption is difficult to satisfy when the robot observes the scene through images. For example, rotating a drawer changes both its appearance to a fixed camera and the direction needed to pull it open. Although the physical rotation is simple, the resulting image transformation depends on the scene geometry and viewpoint and generally cannot be expressed as an image rotation. Existing methods address this difficulty by using point clouds [ 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 ] or projecting observations into representations with known group operations [ 22 , 12 , 6 , 9 ] . These representations make the group operation explicit, but constructing them can require preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. Extending the same approach to a new observation modality can therefore require redesigning how observations are represented and transformed. Thus, even when the relevant symmetry group is known, exploiting it still depends on manually specifying suitable representations and the corresponding observation–action transformations. This motivates a natural question: can we learn the required representations and coupled observation–action transformations directly from environment interaction data? Existing symmetry-discovery methods provide a promising foundation; for example, LaLiGAN [ 23 ] learns nonlinear symmetries of high-dimensional data through latent representations. Applying these approaches to visual control introduces two requirements. First, observations and actions must transform together to preserve their relationships with subsequent observations and rewards. Second, the learned transformations must satisfy the group-operation axioms: applying two transformations successively should agree with applying their composition. Distribution matching alone does not ensure this consistency, and even an exact linear group operation in latent space can lose it after approximate encoding and decoding. These requirements motivate learning coupled observation–action transformations while explicitly regularizing their group consistency. We introduce MIRROR , a framework that learns how a known symmetry group G G operates jointly on observations and actions from offline interaction data in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). The core idea is to match the distributions of original and transformed one-step transition tuples τ = ( o , a , o ′ , r ) \tau=(o,a,o^{\prime},r) , coupling observation and action learning through the observed transitions and rewards. We implement this distribution matching with an adversarial objective, which we call adversarial tuple matching . Identity, compatibility, and invertibility regularizers penalize violations of the group-operation axioms. To represent nonlinear transformations of pixel observations, MIRROR first compresses images with a pretrained, frozen perceptual autoencoder. Separate encoder–decoder pairs then map these perceptual latents and the actions to symmetry latent spaces with fixed linear representations of G G . Both objectives operate on tuples of perceptual latents, actions, and rewards. Learning these mappings from each task’s data allows the same discovery procedure to be used across tasks without manually specifying their coupled observation–action transformations. We evaluate MIRROR on four Robosuite [ 27 ] tabletop manipulation tasks with RGB observations. It achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61 % 61\% reduction in compatibility error relative to our adapted LaLiGAN [ 23 ] baseline. Incorporating the discovered transformations into frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks. Average success increases from 80.48 % 80.48\% to 85.12 % 85.12\% , with the largest per-task gain of 9.66 9.66 percentage points on Cube Dropping. We also apply the framework to heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, repeating symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation before deploying the resulting policy zero-shot on a Kinova GEN3 arm. Our contributions: • Adversarial symmetry discovery in POMDPs: We formulate the discovery of coupled observation–action transformations as adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples ( o , a , o ′ , r ) (o,a,o^{\prime},r) . • Explicit group-consistency regularization: We penalize violations of identity, compatibility, and invertibility, improving aggregate compatibility and invertibility errors over the adapted GAN baselines. • Policy learning with discovered symmetries: We use the learned transformations in a frame-averaged BC policy, improving simulation success rates by up to 9.66 9.66 percentage points over vanilla BC. We also demonstrate the framework with a second observation modality and zero-shot policy deployment on a Kinova GEN3 arm.

sections.heading: Exploiting symmetry in robot policy learning.
sections.text: Symmetry has been extensively studied as an inductive bias for robotic manipulation, yielding consistent gains in sample efficiency and generalization [ 22 , 12 , 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 , 6 , 9 ] . A central limitation is that these methods assume the way the symmetry group operates on observations and actions is known a priori , which rarely holds for visual manipulation tasks. Existing work circumvents this with task-specific observation preprocessing, such as using point clouds from depth cameras [ 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 ] or projecting observations into a representation where the symmetry operates linearly. Concrete instances of the latter include projecting depth images to a top-down heightmap [ 22 ] , inpainting images to make the top-down view equivariant [ 12 ] , mapping fisheye images to a 3D sphere [ 6 ] , and lifting 2D images to 3D ray features [ 9 ] . No single recipe transfers across environments. MIRROR addresses this limitation by learning coupled nonlinear observation–action transformations for a specified group G G from offline interaction data, reducing dependence on manually designed, modality-specific transformations.

sections.heading: Data-driven symmetry discovery.
sections.text: Automatic symmetry discovery identifies unknown symmetries directly from data [ 1 , 13 , 7 ] and has improved downstream tasks such as equation discovery and long-horizon forecasting [ 24 , 23 ] . However, two limitations restrict prior work’s applicability to control in POMDPs. First, prior methods discover symmetries on observations alone, whereas decision-making requires coupled observation–action transformations that preserve the transition structure. Second, prior methods either omit explicit group-consistency regularization entirely [ 2 , 11 , 24 ] or regularize only a subset of the group-operation axioms, as in LaLiGAN [ 23 ] , which regularizes only the identity axiom and accordingly violates the other group-operation axioms in practice. To address both gaps, we discover coupled observation–action transformations from one-step transition tuples τ = ( o , a , o ′ , r ) \tau=(o,a,o^{\prime},r) via adversarial tuple matching, and we explicitly regularize the group-operation axioms (identity, compatibility, invertibility) to encourage the learned transformations to behave as valid group operations.

sections.heading: 4 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 2: Two-stage latent symmetry discovery. Stage 1 trains a perceptual autoencoder ( E o , D o ) (E_{o},D_{o}) to reconstruct observations and then freezes it. In Stage 2, separate symmetry modules encode the perceptual latents ( z , z ′ ) (z,z^{\prime}) and action a a into symmetry spaces, apply fixed linear representations of the same sampled g ∈ G g\in G , and decode the transformed outputs. Adversarial training uses a tuple discriminator to match original and transformed latent transition-tuple distributions, with rewards unchanged. Group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of identity, compatibility, and invertibility. Given a known symmetry group G G and an offline dataset 𝒟 = { ( o , a , o ′ , r ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(o,a,o^{\prime},r)\} from a POMDP, our goal is to learn coupled observation–action transformations ( ϕ o , ϕ a ) (\phi_{o},\phi_{a}) that preserve the transition-tuple distribution and satisfy the group-operation axioms. Joint tuple matching encourages the transformed observations and actions to remain consistent with the recorded transitions and rewards. Figure 2 summarizes MIRROR; Section 4.1 describes the latent parameterization, and Section 4.2 presents the learning objective.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Perceptual autoencoder.
sections.text: To reduce the cost of symmetry discovery from pixel observations, we pretrain a perceptual autoencoder ( E o , D o ) (E_{o},D_{o}) on 𝒟 \mathcal{D} for reconstruction and then freeze it (Appendix C ). sections.text: Distribution matching and group consistency also admit a trivial solution: every group element leaves all observations and actions unchanged. sections.heading: Symmetry-quality metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate the learned transformations with four complementary checks. Symmetry invariance error measures how closely transformed transition tuples match the original data distribution. Identity error checks that applying the identity leaves the input unchanged. Compatibility error measures composition consistency: applying two transformations successively should agree with applying their combination in one step. Invertibility error checks that a transformation followed by its inverse recovers the input. Lower is better for all four metrics; full definitions are in Appendix B.5 .

sections.heading: Baselines and ablations.
sections.text: We adapt two GAN-based baselines to the same tuple formulation and architecture. Within this shared setting, SymGAN uses adversarial tuple matching [ 2 , 24 , 11 ] , while LaLiGAN additionally regularizes identity consistency [ 23 ] . Neither adapted baseline includes compatibility or invertibility regularization. To assess the contribution of each loss term, we remove the adversarial tuple-matching, identity, compatibility, or invertibility term from MIRROR one at a time. We use three training seeds per task and the evaluation angles specified in Appendix B.5 . Figure 5 summarizes all four tasks; per-task results are in Appendix D . sections.heading: Group consistency.
sections.text: Both GAN baselines exhibit substantially higher composition errors: aggregate compatibility error is 1.994 1.994 for SymGAN and 1.838 1.838 for LaLiGAN, versus 0.717 0.717 for MIRROR—a reduction of at least 61 % 61\% (Figure 5 (c); Table 1 ). LaLiGAN’s slightly lower identity error does not translate into consistent composition: reconstructing the input under the identity is insufficient to ensure that different transformations work together. The full model also reduces aggregate invertibility error by at least 39 % 39\% relative to either GAN baseline (Figure 5 (d)). The loss ablations reveal an asymmetry among the group-consistency regularizers. Removing ℒ comp \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}} , while retaining identity and invertibility regularization, increases aggregate compatibility error from 0.717 0.717 to 1.134 1.134 . Removing identity or invertibility regularization produces smaller increases, to 0.818 0.818 and 0.813 0.813 , respectively (Table 1 ). Figure 6: Compatibility error heatmaps on Drawer Opening. Errors compare successive transformations with their composition at all 256 256 ordered pairs of 16 16 equally spaced angles; heatmaps are smoothed for visualization. MIRROR (large left panel), baselines, and single-loss ablations share a color scale (lower is better). MIRROR maintains low error across the evaluated pairs.

sections.heading: Why explicitly regularize composition?
sections.text: This asymmetry is consistent with the logical dependence among the underlying axioms. Appendix A.2 proves that, when satisfied exactly, composition consistency together with either identity or invertibility implies the remaining axiom. In contrast, identity and invertibility together do not imply composition consistency. Composition therefore supplies a constraint on how different transformations combine that reconstruction and inverse checks alone cannot ensure. Figure 6 illustrates this distinction on Drawer Opening. MIRROR maintains low compatibility error across the evaluated angle pairs, while removing ℒ comp \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}} introduces regions of elevated error despite retaining identity and invertibility regularization. Removing ℒ id \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{id}} or ℒ inv \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}} produces smaller changes across the grid. These results support explicitly regularizing composition. The theoretical result concerns exact constraints, so it does not imply that identity and invertibility penalties are interchangeable during training.

sections.heading: 5.3 Do the discovered symmetries improve robot policy learning?
sections.text: Having evaluated symmetry quality, we now test whether the learned transformations benefit policy learning. We use frame-averaged BC [ 14 ] : predict actions from transformed observations, map them back to the original action frame, and average them. Experimental method names use the prefix EBC (equivariant behavior cloning), giving EBC-MIRROR for our transformations. The policy averages over n n transformations from the cyclic subgroup H = C n ⊂ S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) H=C_{n}\subset SO(2) ; construction, training details, and conditions for exact equivariance are given in Appendix E . sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced MIRROR , a framework for learning how a specified symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in pixel-based POMDPs from offline interaction data. We formulate observable symmetry as invariance of the offline one-step transition-tuple distribution. Adversarial tuple matching learns coupled transformations, while identity, compatibility, and invertibility regularization encourages consistency with the group-operation axioms. Across four Robosuite manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61 % 61\% reduction in compatibility error relative to the adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using these transformations in frame-averaged BC yields higher mean success rates on all four tasks than vanilla BC and the hand-designed and GAN-discovered symmetry baselines at H = C 16 H=C_{16} . Gains over vanilla BC reach 9.66 9.66 percentage points on Cube Dropping and 4.64 4.64 percentage points on average. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a Kinova GEN3 arm. Together, these results show that learning coupled observation–action transformations from data can improve visual policy learning without manually specifying how a known symmetry group operates on images and robot commands.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: MIRROR has two scope boundaries worth naming. First, the framework discovers how a group operates on observations and actions but requires the group G G itself to be specified in advance; we view this as a mild assumption in practice, since the relevant group is usually evident from task geometry while its observation–action transformations are what is genuinely hard to specify by hand. Second, MIRROR can only recover symmetries that are already present in the data: if the dataset lacks variation along the symmetry (for example, a fixed scene orientation across all episodes), the discriminator has nothing to match against, and ( ϕ o , ϕ a ) (\phi_{o},\phi_{a}) may collapse toward the identity.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Under the lemma’s assumptions, the perceptual autoencoder is a change of coordinates between 𝒪 ∗ \mathcal{O}_{\ast} and 𝒵 ∗ \mathcal{Z}_{\ast} . An exact latent group operation therefore induces an exact observation-space group operation on the corresponding support. The conclusion depends on the stated inverse and invariance conditions; pretraining and freezing the autoencoder alone does not guarantee them.

sections.heading: Remark (learned approximations).
sections.text: The lemma establishes exact preservation under its stated assumptions. In practice, the perceptual autoencoder is approximately invertible, and the learned latent operation is encouraged to satisfy the group-operation axioms through regularization. Consequently, the learned observation-space operation may exhibit residual axiom violations, which we quantify using the evaluation metrics in Appendix B.5 .

sections.text: We first specify the simulation setup, observation and action coordinates, and per-task reward functions. We then describe offline data collection in Section B.4 , followed by the evaluation metrics and group sampling in Section B.5 .

sections.heading: B.1 Robosuite Setup
sections.text: All four tabletop tasks share the same Robosuite hardware and perception configuration, chosen to mirror our physical platform so that the same observation and action interfaces can be reused in the sim-to-real study of Appendix F.1 . The simulated arm is a 7 7 -DoF Kinova GEN3 manipulator equipped with a Robotiq 2F85 parallel-jaw gripper, matching the real robot used for zero-shot transfer. Rather than adopting one of Robosuite’s built-in camera presets, we calibrate the simulator camera against the real workspace: we first mount an Intel RealSense D435 in front of the table and run a standard eye-to-hand calibration to recover its intrinsic matrix and its extrinsic pose with respect to the robot base, and we then transcribe both matrices into the simulator so that the virtual camera reproduces the same viewpoint, field of view, and projection geometry as the physical sensor. This calibration-driven setup yields RGB observations whose camera geometry is aligned between simulation and the real robot, eliminating viewpoint-induced sim-to-real gap before any policy transfer.

sections.heading: B.4 Offline Dataset and Behavior Policy
sections.text: For each task, we collect 100,000 100{,}000 one-step transition tuples ( o , a , o ′ , r ) (o,a,o^{\prime},r) for training and 10,000 10{,}000 for evaluation, as described in Section 5 . Each tuple contains the current and next RGB observations, the normalized end-effector command, and the task-specific reward vector defined above. The behavior policy used to collect the offline interaction data for all four tasks is a simple finite-state-machine controller that drives the robot end-effector through a sequence of task-specific waypoints using proportional pose control. The waypoint sequence for each task is listed below.

sections.heading: Appendix C Symmetry-Discovery Implementation
sections.text: This appendix specifies the network architectures (Section C.1 ), fixed group representations (Section C.2 ), training objectives and procedure (Section C.3 ), and hyperparameters (Section C.4 ) for symmetry discovery. Evaluation metrics and evaluation-time group sampling are described in Appendix B.5 , and the frame-averaged BC policy is described in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Perceptual autoencoder ( E o , D o ) (E_{o},D_{o}) (Stage 1).
sections.text: We instantiate the perceptual autoencoder as a convolutional spherical autoencoder [ 26 ] that maps each workspace observation to a unit-norm perceptual latent and back, providing the smooth perceptual latent space on which Stage 2 symmetry discovery operates. The network accepts a channel-first C × 128 × 128 C\times 128\times 128 tensor with C = 3 C=3 for the raw RGB images used in the simulation-only experiments and C = 2 C=2 for the stacked heightmap and segmentation mask used in the sim-to-real pipeline. The encoder is a five-stage convolutional tower with channel widths 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 4,8,16,32,64 , SiLU activations, and layer normalization, interleaved with four average-pooling downsamples that produce a 64 × 8 × 8 64\times 8\times 8 bottleneck. A linear projection followed by ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization then sends this bottleneck to a perceptual latent z = E o ​ ( o ) ∈ 𝕊 15 z=E_{o}(o)\in\mathbb{S}^{15} with ambient dimension d z = 16 d_{z}=16 . The decoder mirrors this structure: a linear expansion lifts z z back to a 64 × 8 × 8 64\times 8\times 8 feature map, bilinear-upsampling blocks with channel widths 128 , 64 , 32 , 16 , 8 128,64,32,16,8 progressively restore spatial resolution, and a final 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution followed by a tanh \tanh activation and per-channel range de-normalization recovers the input tensor.

sections.heading: Symmetry modules ( E z , D z ) (E_{z},D_{z}) and ( E a , D a ) (E_{a},D_{a}) (Stage 2).
sections.text: The Stage 2 symmetry modules are two residual MLP autoencoders that wrap the Stage 1 perceptual latent and the environment action in their own learnable spherical symmetry latent spaces. The observation symmetry encoder E z E_{z} maps the Stage 1 perceptual latent z ∈ 𝕊 15 z\in\mathbb{S}^{15} to an observation symmetry latent u = E z ​ ( z ) u=E_{z}(z) with dimension d u = 64 d_{u}=64 , and the observation symmetry decoder D z D_{z} maps it back to 𝕊 15 \mathbb{S}^{15} . The action symmetry encoder E a E_{a} maps each normalized environment action a ∈ 𝒜 ⊆ [ − 1 , 1 ] d a a\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq[-1,1]^{d_{a}} to an action symmetry latent v = E a ​ ( a ) v=E_{a}(a) with dimension d v = 16 d_{v}=16 , and the action symmetry decoder D a D_{a} maps it back to normalized action coordinates. All four modules share a common MLP template. Each encoder consists of a linear projection Linear ⁡ ( d in , 128 ) \mathrm{Linear}(d_{\mathrm{in}},128) , a single width- 128 128 residual block, and a final GELU \mathrm{GELU} – Linear ⁡ ( 128 , d lat ) \mathrm{Linear}(128,d_{\mathrm{lat}}) projection. Each decoder is wider: a linear expansion Linear ⁡ ( d lat , 256 ) \mathrm{Linear}(d_{\mathrm{lat}},256) , a single width- 256 256 residual block, and a final GELU \mathrm{GELU} – Linear ⁡ ( 256 , d out ) \mathrm{Linear}(256,d_{\mathrm{out}}) projection. The observation branch uses d in = d out = d z d_{\mathrm{in}}=d_{\mathrm{out}}=d_{z} and d lat = d u d_{\mathrm{lat}}=d_{u} ; the action branch uses d in = d out = d a d_{\mathrm{in}}=d_{\mathrm{out}}=d_{a} and d lat = d v d_{\mathrm{lat}}=d_{v} . Every residual block applies LayerNorm \mathrm{LayerNorm} – GELU \mathrm{GELU} – Linear \mathrm{Linear} – LayerNorm \mathrm{LayerNorm} – GELU \mathrm{GELU} – Linear \mathrm{Linear} with an additive skip connection, and we use neither spectral normalization nor orthogonal parametrization.

sections.heading: Normalization and initialization.
sections.text: All Stage 2 symmetry latents are projected onto the unit hypersphere, and the output of D z D_{z} is additionally projected back onto the Stage 1 perceptual latent space 𝕊 15 \mathbb{S}^{15} . Keeping transformed perceptual latents on the same sphere as the original latents facilitates adversarial tuple matching. Linear layers use Kaiming initialization tuned for GELU activations, except for the final encoder projection, which uses Xavier-normal initialization with gain 0.01 0.01 and zero bias. The decomposition of each symmetry latent into rotating and invariant coordinates is specified in Section C.2 .

sections.heading: Discriminator f ψ f_{\psi} .
sections.text: The tuple discriminator f ψ f_{\psi} is a spectral-normalized MLP with two scoring heads: a transition head f ψ mdp f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{mdp}} that scores latent transition tuples jointly and an auxiliary marginal head f ψ obs f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{obs}} that scores perceptual latents on their own. The transition head ingests a latent transition tuple ( z , a , z ′ , r ) (z,a,z^{\prime},r) , where z , z ′ ∈ 𝕊 15 z,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{S}^{15} are Stage 1 perceptual latents, a ∈ ℝ d a a\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} is the environment action, and r r is the per-task vector-valued reward defined in Appendix B.3 . Each of the four components is first embedded into ℝ 32 \mathbb{R}^{32} by a dedicated spectral-normalized linear subnet, and the four embeddings are concatenated to form a 128 128 -dimensional tuple feature. This feature is then mapped to a scalar logit via three spectral-normalized linear layers, interleaved with leaky ReLU activations. The marginal head reuses the same backbone but starts from a single ℝ 128 \mathbb{R}^{128} embedding of a perceptual latent; we apply it independently to z z and z ′ z^{\prime} and concatenate the two scalar scores to form its output.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Perceptual pretraining.
sections.text: We train ( E o , D o ) (E_{o},D_{o}) on observations from 𝒟 \mathcal{D} with a normalized L 1 L_{1} reconstruction loss after an initial L 2 L_{2} warm-up. A latent cycle-consistency term encourages E o ​ ( D o ​ ( z ) ) ≈ z E_{o}(D_{o}(z))\approx z . When enabled, a perceptual discriminator supplies adversarial and feature-matching losses to sharpen reconstruction texture; their weights are introduced with a linear warm-up. The warm-up durations and optimization settings are collected in Section C.4 .

sections.heading: Transition to Stage 2.
sections.text: After pretraining, we freeze ( E o , D o ) (E_{o},D_{o}) and encode each transition tuple τ = ( o , a , o ′ , r ) \tau=(o,a,o^{\prime},r) from the offline dataset as a latent transition tuple t = ( z , a , z ′ , r ) t=(z,a,z^{\prime},r) with z = E o ​ ( o ) z=E_{o}(o) and z ′ = E o ​ ( o ′ ) z^{\prime}=E_{o}(o^{\prime}) . For a sampled g g , the transformed tuple Φ z ​ ( g , t ) \Phi_{z}(g,t) applies ϕ z \phi_{z} to both perceptual latents and ϕ a \phi_{a} to the action, leaving the reward unchanged.

sections.text: We implement the adversarial tuple-matching objective of Eq. ( 1 ) as a multi-head hinge-GAN on raw logits, applied to each scoring head as an independent discriminator and summed in a multi-discriminator fashion. Concretely, the transition head contributes the hinge discriminator loss ℒ disc mdp = 1 2 ​ 𝔼 t ​ [ max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − f ψ mdp ​ ( t ) ) ] + 1 2 ​ 𝔼 t , g ​ [ max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 + f ψ mdp ​ ( Φ z ​ ( g , t ) ) ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{mdp}}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\max(0,\,1-f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{mdp}}(t))\right]\;+\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{t,g}\!\left[\max(0,\,1+f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{mdp}}(\Phi_{z}(g,t)))\right], and the marginal head contributes the same hinge form applied independently to each perceptual latent in the tuple, treating z z and ϕ z ​ ( g , z ) \phi_{z}(g,z) as a real/fake pair and likewise for z ′ z^{\prime} and ϕ z ​ ( g , z ′ ) \phi_{z}(g,z^{\prime}) . The discriminator minimizes the total discriminator loss ℒ disc = ℒ disc mdp + ℒ disc obs \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{disc}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{mdp}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{obs}} . The symmetry modules act as the generator and minimize ℒ gen = − 𝔼 t , g ​ [ f ψ ​ ( Φ z ​ ( g , t ) ) ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}=-\,\mathbb{E}_{t,g}[f_{\psi}(\Phi_{z}(g,t))] , summed across heads in the same multi-head fashion. This loss is the hinge realization of the ℒ adv \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}} term that enters the symmetry modules’ total loss in Eq. ( 3 ). The symmetry modules additionally minimize the identity, compatibility, and invertibility regularizers of Eq. ( 2 ), and the nontriviality penalty ℒ nt \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nt}} between z z and ϕ z ​ ( g , z ) \phi_{z}(g,z) and between z ′ z^{\prime} and ϕ z ​ ( g , z ′ ) \phi_{z}(g,z^{\prime}) . Their weighted sum with the adversarial tuple-matching loss is specified in Eq. ( 3 ).

sections.heading: Input normalization and alternating updates.
sections.text: Perceptual latents and actions are passed to f ψ f_{\psi} without further normalization, since the latents already lie on 𝕊 15 \mathbb{S}^{15} by construction and the environment actions are already normalized to [ − 1 , 1 ] d a [-1,1]^{d_{a}} ; reward components are standardized to zero mean and unit variance across 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Stabilization relies on the discriminator’s spectral normalization together with gradient clipping; we use neither a gradient penalty nor an R 1 R_{1} regularizer. The discriminator and the symmetry modules are updated one-to-one: one discriminator step follows every symmetry-module step.

sections.heading: Appendix E Frame-Averaged Behavior Cloning
sections.text: This appendix describes EBC-MIRROR, the frame-averaged BC policy built on the discovered transformations ( ϕ o , ϕ a ) (\phi_{o},\phi_{a}) . We present the policy construction and its equivariance conditions (Section E.1 ), architecture and training objective (Section E.2 ), baselines and evaluation protocol (Section E.3 ), and subgroup-size results (Section E.4 ). The RGB results support Section 5.3 ; the sim-to-real experiments are collected in Appendix F .

sections.heading: E.1 Frame-Averaged Policy and Equivariance Conditions
sections.text: Let H H be a finite subgroup of G G and let f θ f_{\theta} be a base policy network that maps observations to actions. Following the frame-averaging construction [ 14 ] , we use the discovered transformations ϕ o \phi_{o} and ϕ a \phi_{a} to define π θ ​ ( o ) := 1 | H | ​ ∑ g ∈ H ϕ a ​ ( g − 1 , f θ ​ ( ϕ o ​ ( g , o ) ) ) . \pi_{\theta}(o)~:=~\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{g\in H}\phi_{a}\!\left(g^{-1},\,f_{\theta}(\phi_{o}(g,o))\right). (20) Intuitively, we (i) transform the input observation by g g , (ii) predict an action in that transformed frame via f θ f_{\theta} , (iii) map the predicted action back with ϕ a ​ ( g − 1 , ⋅ ) \phi_{a}(g^{-1},\cdot) , and finally (iv) average over g ∈ H g\in H . Our experiments use G = S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) G=SO(2) and average over a finite cyclic subgroup H = C n ⊂ S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) H=C_{n}\subset SO(2) . The equivariance result below concerns this subgroup H H .

sections.heading: Conditions for exact equivariance.
sections.text: Assume that ϕ o \phi_{o} and ϕ a \phi_{a} satisfy the group-operation axioms exactly on the relevant supports, and that all transformations and averages below are well-defined. We additionally require the action transformation to commute with arithmetic averaging: for every h ∈ H h\in H and admissible collection of actions { a k } k ∈ H \{a_{k}\}_{k\in H} , ϕ a ​ ( h , 1 | H | ​ ∑ k ∈ H a k ) = 1 | H | ​ ∑ k ∈ H ϕ a ​ ( h , a k ) . \phi_{a}\!\left(h,\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{k\in H}a_{k}\right)=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{k\in H}\phi_{a}(h,a_{k}). (21) This condition holds, for example, when each ϕ a ​ ( h , ⋅ ) \phi_{a}(h,\cdot) is affine and the averages remain in the action domain. Under these assumptions, reindexing the sum by k = g ∘ h k=g\circ h gives π θ ​ ( ϕ o ​ ( h , o ) ) \displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(\phi_{o}(h,o)) = 1 | H | ​ ∑ g ∈ H ϕ a ​ ( g − 1 , f θ ​ ( ϕ o ​ ( g ∘ h , o ) ) ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{g\in H}\phi_{a}\!\left(g^{-1},f_{\theta}(\phi_{o}(g\circ h,o))\right) = 1 | H | ​ ∑ k ∈ H ϕ a ​ ( h , ϕ a ​ ( k − 1 , f θ ​ ( ϕ o ​ ( k , o ) ) ) ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{k\in H}\phi_{a}\!\left(h,\phi_{a}\!\left(k^{-1},f_{\theta}(\phi_{o}(k,o))\right)\right) = ϕ a ​ ( h , π θ ​ ( o ) ) . \displaystyle=\phi_{a}(h,\pi_{\theta}(o)). The first two equalities use the exact group-operation axioms, and the last uses Eq. ( 21 ). Thus, Eq. ( 20 ) defines an H H -equivariant policy under the stated conditions.

sections.text: In MIRROR, ϕ a ​ ( g , ⋅ ) = D a ​ ( ρ a ​ ( g ) ​ E a ​ ( ⋅ ) ) \phi_{a}(g,\cdot)=D_{a}(\rho_{a}(g)E_{a}(\cdot)) is nonlinear, and the learned coupled observation–action transformations are regularized to satisfy the group-operation axioms. sections.heading: E.2 Policy Architecture and Training Objective
sections.text: We instantiate f θ f_{\theta} with a pretrained ResNet-18 backbone followed by a two-layer MLP with 64 hidden units per layer and ReLU activations. The same base policy is applied to every transformed observation in Eq. ( 20 ). During BC training, we hold the perceptual autoencoder and the observation and action symmetry modules fixed and optimize the base-policy parameters θ \theta . The mean-squared BC loss is applied to the final averaged action: min θ ⁡ ℒ EBC ​ ( θ ) := 𝔼 ( o , a ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ ‖ π θ ​ ( o ) − a ‖ 2 2 ] . \min_{\theta}~\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EBC}}(\theta)~:=~\mathbb{E}_{(o,a)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\,\|\pi_{\theta}(o)-a\|_{2}^{2}\,\Big]. (22) Gradients propagate through the fixed action transformations to train f θ f_{\theta} within the frame-averaged policy.

sections.heading: E.3 Baselines and Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate policies by rolling them out on the four RGB Robosuite tasks described in Appendix B and report per-task episodic success rates and their average. We compare vanilla BC , which omits frame averaging, with four frame-averaged BC variants that use different coupled observation–action transformations. EBC-MIRROR uses our discovered transformations; EBC-SymGAN and EBC-LaLiGAN reuse the GAN-discovered transformations from Section 5 ; and EBC-ExSym uses the hand-designed Extrapolated Symmetry [ 21 ] . ExSym rotates images in pixel space and applies the following transformation directly to normalized action coordinates: ( Δ ​ x , Δ ​ y , Δ ​ z , Δ ​ ψ , Δ ​ w ) ↦ ( R ⁡ ( θ g ) ​ ( Δ ​ x , Δ ​ y ) ⊤ , Δ ​ z , Δ ​ ψ , Δ ​ w ) , (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z,\Delta\psi,\Delta w)\;\mapsto\;\big(R(\theta_{g})(\Delta x,\Delta y)^{\!\top},\,\Delta z,\,\Delta\psi,\,\Delta w\big), where R ⁡ ( θ g ) R(\theta_{g}) is the 2 2 D rotation matrix. This rotates only the planar translation components; Δ ​ ψ \Delta\psi or Δ ​ w \Delta w is omitted when the task has no yaw or gripper control. For all frame-averaged BC variants we sweep the subgroup size n = | H | n=|H| with H = C n H=C_{n} and n ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } n\in\{2,4,8,16\} .

sections.heading: Appendix F Sim-to-Real Experiments
sections.text: This appendix details the sim-to-real experiments in Section 6 . We describe the hardware and observation preprocessing, specify the training and deployment protocol, and then report simulation and real-world results. Qualitative visualizations of the learned observation–action transformations follow the quantitative evaluation.

sections.heading: F.1.1 Hardware Setup
sections.text: We deploy the learned policy on a 7 7 -DoF Kinova GEN3 manipulator equipped with a Robotiq 2F85 parallel-jaw gripper. Visual observations are provided by an Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera mounted on a fixed stand in front of the workspace. The camera-to-robot extrinsics are obtained once via standard eye-to-hand calibration and reused across all tasks.

sections.heading: F.1.2 Observation Preprocessing
sections.text: The policy consumes a heightmap and a target-object segmentation mask rather than raw RGB. Figure 16 illustrates the preprocessing pipeline, and main-paper Figure 8 (e,f) compares the resulting real-world observation against its simulated counterpart.

sections.heading: Heightmap.
sections.text: We project the depth image into a top-down heightmap of the workspace and clip the height values to the range [ 0 , 0.3 ] ​ m [0,\,0.3]\,\text{m} above the table surface. The clipped heights are then linearly rescaled to [ 0 , 255 ] [0,\,255] and stored as an 8 8 -bit single-channel image, matching the dynamic range used in simulation.

sections.heading: Segmentation mask.
sections.text: The target-object segmentation mask is obtained with SAM 2 [ 15 ] , prompted using a height-derived foreground prior. The resulting binary segmentation mask is stacked with the heightmap to form the final policy input. Figure 16: Real-world observation preprocessing. Depth is projected into a top-down heightmap, and a height-derived foreground prior prompts SAM 2 to segment the RGB image. The heightmap is clipped to [ 0 , 0.3 ] [0,0.3] m above the table and rescaled to an 8 8 -bit image, then stacked with the binary segmentation mask to form the two-channel policy input.

sections.heading: F.2 Training and Deployment Protocol
sections.text: For real-world deployment, we use heightmap and segmentation-mask observations (Appendix F.1.2 ), similar to Lin et al. [10] . We run Stage 1 and Stage 2 symmetry discovery in simulation on this modality using the procedure in Appendix C , then freeze the resulting perceptual autoencoder and the observation and action symmetry modules. We train a separate EBC-MIRROR policy entirely in simulation using these frozen transformations for frame averaging. The base policy architecture follows Appendix E.2 , with its input encoder adapted to the two-channel input, and the BC objective remains Eq. ( 22 ). Relative to the RGB experiments, the changes are the observation modality, the corresponding input adaptation, and the observation–action transformations learned for this modality. The resulting policy is deployed zero-shot on the real robot using the hardware and preprocessing in Appendix F.1 . We report simulation performance in Appendix F.3 and real-world outcomes in Appendix F.4 .

sections.heading: F.3 Simulation Results with Heightmap and Segmentation-Mask Observations
sections.text: We evaluate behavior-cloning policies in simulation using the same heightmap and segmentation-mask observation modality used at real-world deployment (Appendix F.1.2 ). This isolates the contribution of the discovered symmetry from the observation-modality change: every policy in Table 11 consumes the same heightmap and segmentation-mask input, and the only difference between rows is whether the discovered observation–action transformations ( ϕ o , ϕ a ) (\phi_{o},\phi_{a}) are used for frame-averaged BC (EBC-MIRROR, Appendix E.1 ) and, if so, with which finite cyclic subgroup H = C n H=C_{n} . Each cell reports mean and standard deviation of episodic success rate over three seeds and the same evaluation protocol used in Appendix E.3 .

sections.heading: Results.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17422v1 [cs.RO] 12 Oct 2026 MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data Shiqi Liu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Yihang Yao Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Peide Huang Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Mengdi Xu Affiliation: Stanford University Ding Zhao Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation–action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 𝟔𝟏 % \mathbf{61\%} reduction in compatibility error—which measures consistency under transformation composition—relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48 % 80.48\% to 85.12 % 85.12\% , with per-task gains up to 9.66 \mathbf{9.66} percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io . Figure 1: Overview of MIRROR. From offline robot interaction data, MIRROR learns how a specified symmetry group jointly transforms observations and actions. Adversarial matching encourages transformed transition tuples to preserve the original data distribution, while group-consistency regularization encourages identity, composition, and inverse consistency. The examples on the right illustrate the learned coupling: transforming a scene also transforms its associated robot command, mapping an observation–action pair ( o , a ) (o,a) to corresponding pairs ( g ⋅ o , g ⋅ a ) (g\cdot o,g\cdot a) . Keywords: Symmetry Discovery, Equivariant Policy Learning, Robot Manipulation 1 Introduction Symmetry can improve sample efficiency and generalization in robot policy learning by allowing experience to be shared across equivalent task configurations [ 22 , 12 , 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 , 6 , 9 ] . Exploiting this structure requires coupled observation–action transformations, which existing symmetry-aware methods typically assume are known. This assumption is difficult to satisfy when the robot observes the scene through images. For example, rotating a drawer changes both its appearance to a fixed camera and the direction needed to pull it open. Although the physical rotation is simple, the resulting image transformation depends on the scene geometry and viewpoint and generally cannot be expressed as an image rotation. Existing methods address this difficulty by using point clouds [ 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 ] or projecting observations into representations with known group operations [ 22 , 12 , 6 , 9 ] . These representations make the group operation explicit, but constructing them can require preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. Extending the same approach to a new observation modality can therefore require redesigning how observations are represented and transformed. Thus, even when the relevant symmetry group is known, exploiting it still depends on manually specifying suitable representations and the corresponding observation–action transformations. This motivates a natural question: can we learn the required representations and coupled observation–action transformations directly from environment interaction data? Existing symmetry-discovery methods provide a promising foundation; for example, LaLiGAN [ 23 ] learns nonlinear symmetries of high-dimensional data through latent representations. Applying these approaches to visual control introduces two requirements. First, observations and actions must transform together to preserve their relationships with subsequent observations and rewards. Second, the learned transformations must satisfy the group-operation axioms: applying two transformations successively should agree with applying their composition. Distribution matching alone does not ensure this consistency, and even an exact linear group operation in latent space can lose it after approximate encoding and decoding. These requirements motivate learning coupled observation–action transformations while explicitly regularizing their group consistency. We introduce MIRROR , a framework that learns how a known symmetry group G G operates jointly on observations and actions from offline interaction data in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). The core idea is to match the distributions of original and transformed one-step transition tuples τ = ( o , a , o ′ , r ) \tau=(o,a,o^{\prime},r) , coupling observation and action learning through the observed transitions and rewards. We implement this distribution matching with an adversarial objective, which we call adversarial tuple matching . Identity, compatibility, and invertibility regularizers penalize violations of the group-operation axioms. To represent nonlinear transformations of pixel observations, MIRROR first compresses images with a pretrained, frozen perceptual autoencoder. Separate encoder–decoder pairs then map these perceptual latents and the actions to symmetry latent spaces with fixed linear representations of G G . Both objectives operate on tuples of perceptual latents, actions, and rewards. Learning these mappings from each task’s data allows the same discovery procedure to be used across tasks without manually specifying their coupled observation–action transformations. We evaluate MIRROR on four Robosuite [ 27 ] tabletop manipulation tasks with RGB observations. It achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61 % 61\% reduction in compatibility error relative to our adapted LaLiGAN [ 23 ] baseline. Incorporating the discovered transformations into frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks. Average success increases from 80.48 % 80.48\% to 85.12 % 85.12\% , with the largest per-task gain of 9.66 9.66 percentage points on Cube Dropping. We also apply the framework to heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, repeating symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation before deploying the resulting policy zero-shot on a Kinova GEN3 arm. Our contributions: • Adversarial symmetry discovery in POMDPs: We formulate the discovery of coupled observation–action transformations as adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples ( o , a , o ′ , r ) (o,a,o^{\prime},r) . • Explicit group-consistency regularization: We penalize violations of identity, compatibility, and invertibility, improving aggregate compatibility and invertibility errors over the adapted GAN baselines. • Policy learning with discovered symmetries: We use the learned transformations in a frame-averaged BC policy, improving simulation success rates by up to 9.66 9.66 percentage points over vanilla BC. We also demonstrate the framework with a second observation modality and zero-shot policy deployment on a Kinova GEN3 arm. 2 Related Work Exploiting symmetry in robot policy learning. Symmetry has been extensively studied as an inductive bias for robotic manipulation, yielding consistent gains in sample efficiency and generalization [ 22 , 12 , 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 , 6 , 9 ] . A central limitation is that these methods assume the way the symmetry group operates on observations and actions is known a priori , which rarely holds for visual manipulation tasks. Existing work circumvents this with task-specific observation preprocessing, such as using point clouds from depth cameras [ 18 , 8 , 3 , 25 , 20 , 5 ] or projecting observations into a representation where the symmetry operates linearly. Concrete instances of the latter include projecting depth images to a top-down heightmap [ 22 ] , inpainting images to make the top-down view equivariant [ 12 ] , mapping fisheye images to a 3D sphere [ 6 ] , and lifting 2D images to 3D ray features [ 9 ] . No single recipe transfers across environments. MIRROR addresses this limitation by learning coupled nonlinear observation–action transformations for a specified group G G from offline interaction data, reducing dependence on manually designed, modality-specific transformations. Data-driven symmetry discovery. Automatic symmetry discovery identifies unknown symmetries directly from data [ 1 , 13 , 7 ] and has improved downstream tasks such as equation discovery and long-horizon forecasting [ 24 , 23 ] . However, two limitations restrict prior work’s applicability to control in POMDPs. First, prior methods discover symmetries on observations alone, whereas decision-making requires coupled observation–action transformations that preserve the transition structure. Second, prior methods either omit explicit group-consistency regularization entirely [ 2 , 11 , 24 ] or regularize only a subset of the group-operation axioms, as in LaLiGAN [ 23 ] , which regularizes only the identity axiom and accordingly violates the other group-operation axioms in practice. To address both gaps, we discover coupled observation–action transformations from one-step transition tuples τ = ( o , a , o ′ , r ) \tau=(o,a,o^{\prime},r) via adversarial tuple matching, and we explicitly regularize the group-operation axioms (identity, compatibility, invertibility) to encourage the learned transformations to behave as valid group operations. 3 Preliminary Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. We next evaluate whether these transformations preserve the data distribution and satisfy the group-operation axioms. 5.2 How accurately does MIRROR recover observation–action symmetries? Symmetry-quality metrics. We evaluate the learned transformations with four complementary checks. Symmetry invariance error measures how closely transformed transition tuples match the original data distribution. Identity error checks that applying the identity leaves the input unchanged. Compatibility error measures composition consistency: applying two transformations successively should agree with applying their combination in one step. Invertibility error checks that a transformation followed by its inverse recovers the input. Lower is better for all four metrics; full definitions are in Appendix B.5 . Baselines and ablations. We adapt two GAN-based baselines to the same tuple formulation and architecture. Within this shared setting, SymGAN uses adversarial tuple matching [ 2 , 24 , 11 ] , while LaLiGAN additionally regularizes identity consistency [ 23 ] . We formulate observable symmetry as invariance of the offline one-step transition-tuple distribution. Adversarial tuple matching learns coupled transformations, while identity, compatibility, and invertibility regularization encourages consistency with the group-operation axioms. Across four Robosuite manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61 % 61\% reduction in compatibility error relative to the adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using these transformations in frame-averaged BC yields higher mean success rates on all four tasks than vanilla BC and the hand-designed and GAN-discovered symmetry baselines at H = C 16 H=C_{16} . Gains over vanilla BC reach 9.66 9.66 percentage points on Cube Dropping and 4.64 4.64 percentage points on average. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a Kinova GEN3 arm. Together, these results show that learning coupled observation–action transformations from data can improve visual policy learning without manually specifying how a known symmetry group operates on images and robot commands. 8 Limitations MIRROR has two scope boundaries worth naming. First, the framework discovers how a group operates on observations and actions but requires the group G G itself to be specified in advance; we view this as a mild assumption in practice, since the relevant group is usually evident from task geometry while its observation–action transformations are what is genuinely hard to specify by hand. Second, MIRROR can only recover symmetries that are already present in the data: if the dataset lacks variation along the symmetry (for example, a fixed scene orientation across all episodes), the discriminator has nothing to match against, and ( ϕ o , ϕ a ) (\phi_{o},\phi_{a}) may collapse toward the identity.
